name: Unwholesome food (apathya) for the practitioner
description: Foods the haṭha texts forbid to the yogin: the bitter, sour, pungent, salty and hot; green vegetables, sour gruel, oil, sesame, mustard; liquor, fish and meat; curds and buttermilk; horse-gram, garlic and asafoetida; food reheated, dry, stale, putrid, over-hot or over-cold; overeating.
antidotes: wholesome food: wheat, rice, barley, milk, ghee, honey, mung, pure water (HYP 1.62-63)

name: Mortification of the body (kāyakleśa)
description: Ascetic practices that torment the body — early-morning (cold) bathing, fasting, eating once a day or not at all — which the haṭha texts tell the beginner to avoid (Gorakṣa's saying in HYP 1.61; GS 5.31; ŚS 3.33 lists early bathing and fasting among what obstructs yoga). Brahmānanda glosses the 'clinging to rules' (niyamāgraha) of HYP 1.15 with the same examples.
antidotes: moderate, regular practice as the guru teaches

equivalents.note: Brahmānanda explains niyamāgraha (HYP 1.15) as cold bathing at dawn, eating at night, eating only fruit — the same mortifications the Gorakṣa verse (HYP 1.61) forbids.

name: The sun's swallowing of the moon's nectar (the cause of ageing)
description: The nectar that drips from the moon at the palate or crown is swallowed by the sun, the fire at the navel, and so the body grows old and falls under death's power; the throat lock, the inverted posture and khecarī are taught to prevent this.
notes: The doctrine behind it is U28's cpt:sun-moon-fire.

name: Practice learned from texts without a guru
description: The haṭha texts hold that the techniques succeed only when received from a guru: knowledge from the guru's mouth is potent, otherwise it is fruitless, powerless and brings great suffering (ŚS 3.11); the inverting technique is known from the guru's instruction, not from millions of treatises (HYP 3.78); khecarī requires the guru's mantra (Khecarīvidyā).
antidotes: receiving instruction from a qualified guru and serving him (ŚS 3.12-15)
